walkthroughs.body_html:
Philosophy of Religion: Ancient Philosophical Influences (Plato, Aristotle) — a core area of A-Level Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Philosophy of Religion: Ancient Philosophical Influences (Plato, Aristotle) brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Philosophy of Religion: Ancient Philosophical Influences (Plato, Aristotle).

mcqs.q: In the Analogy of the Cave, what do the shadows represent?
options: The world of appearances that people mistake for reality
The Forms themselves
The philosopher's enlightenment
The sun outside the cave
The purpose or telos for which a thing exists
The matter a thing is made from
The agent that brought it about
Its shape or definition

mcqs.q: How does Aristotle's Prime Mover move the universe?
options: As a final cause, attracting motion while itself remaining unchanged
By physically pushing the planets
By creating the world from nothing at a moment in time
By intervening through miracles

mcqs.q: For Plato, where does true knowledge come from?
options: Reason grasping the eternal Forms
The five senses alone
Revelation recorded in scripture
Trial and error experiment

mcqs.q: Is Aristotle's Prime Mover the same as the Christian creator God?
options: Aristotle's Prime Mover is simply the God of the Bible under another name.
The Prime Mover is the engine Aristotle built to model the heavens.
No - the Prime Mover does not create from nothing, does not know or love the world, and moves it only as a final cause; later thinkers like Aquinas adapted rather than copied the idea.
Plato believed the physical world is the only reality.

mcqs.q: Did Plato think the physical world is evil and worthless?
options: Plato taught that the material world is wicked and to be hated.
No - it is less real than the Forms and cannot give true knowledge, but it participates in the Forms and is ordered toward the Good; Plato is not a Gnostic despiser of matter.
Plato believed the physical world is the only reality.
The Forms are physical objects stored in a temple in Athens.

mcqs.q: Are Plato's Forms just concepts inside human minds?
options: The Prime Mover is the engine Aristotle built to model the heavens.
The Forms are physical objects stored in a temple in Athens.
No - Plato held the Forms are mind-independent realities; our concepts are attempts to grasp them, and particulars merely participate in them.
The Forms are simply ideas that humans invent and share.
